name: attorney-client
intent: Grant a named collaborator a deliberately narrow compile-time view of a class's private interface by making an attorney the client's sole friend; the attorney forwards selected operations or re-exports selected private nested types (often through controlled public typedefs), while unrelated private members and the public contract remain closed.
problem: A C++ collaborator may need one private hook, constructor, iterator adapter or nested implementation type, but a friend class receives every private and protected member. Making the hook public leaks it to every caller; publishing a std::list<T>::iterator or the container type leaks representation and its invalidation contract; pImpl hides representation from everyone but does not grant one collaborator a typed privileged view. The missing mechanism is a small attorney contract that names exactly the operations or nested types this collaborator may use without turning the private interface into a second public API.
context: Object-oriented code whose encapsulation boundary is a class and whose language offers class- or scope-level access control but no per-collaborator grant - C++ with friend declarations, Java/C#/Kotlin with package, assembly or module access, and their test- and library-extension scenarios. It applies at object scope, where one type owns the implementation and one named collaborator needs a slice of it, and it is a source-level structuring device checked by the compiler, never a runtime protection mechanism.
benefits: Minimum privilege per collaborator: the requestor sees exactly the operations or intentionally aliased nested types the grantor chose to expose while the rest of the private interface stays unreachable - a blanket friend declaration or a public member would hand over everything at once.

The un-granted implementation stays free to change: a private member that is not part of the attorney's surface can be renamed, re-signed or removed without breaking the requestor, which is the coupling the idiom exists to reduce.

The grant is explicit and reviewable: it is one small class whose own interface is private, so a reviewer can read the entire grant in a few lines instead of auditing which classes are friends of what.

Granularity composes: several attorneys can carve a class's internals into disjoint cohesive groups, and one attorney can mediate between several grantors, keeping every requestor's dependency on the narrow surface.

The classic realizations cost nothing at run time: the forwarding members are inline static one-liners that the compiler erases, so the price is source lines - and it removes the temptation of #define private public style test hacks in the build.
tradeoffs: Boilerplate that must track the client: every granted operation needs a forwarding member duplicating the private signature, and a signature change that still converts (int to double, a new default parameter) compiles while silently forwarding something else until a call breaks.

The attorney itself holds unlimited access: the underlying friendship (or equivalent grant) is all-or-nothing at the attorney, so one careless public member - or a member added later - widens the grant to everything the attorney can reach.

Compile-time only and defeatable at source level: macro tricks, reflection, debuggers and binary patching bypass it, so it must never be sold as a security boundary against an adversary, only as encapsulation against accident.

Coupling in the other direction: the attorney and the requestor become tied to the client's private interface and can no longer be distributed or reused without it - the friend class cannot be shipped without the class that befriends it.

The seam is invisible to consumers and erodes quietly: nothing in the public API shows that an attorney exists, so later contributors add public members or new friends instead of extending the attorney, and the narrow grant decays into several parallel grants.
The dominant real-world use - letting tests reach private state - encourages white-box tests coupled to implementation details, which resist every later refactoring of the class under test.

Constrained friend templates interact poorly with access control in some compilers: Clang has open bugs (llvm/llvm-project#58859, #145505) where a requires clause on a friend template causes the compiler to 'forget' the friendship relationship during constraint checking, silently breaking private access that GCC and MSVC accept. Avoid friend declarations with concept or requires clauses when private member access is needed.

An intentionally public nested-type alias is still a leak if the attorney or its header is broadly available: every includer can name that type and use its public members, so caller restriction requires a private attorney header or private forwarding functions.

participants.responsibility: Owns the private implementation, refuses to expose it publicly, and declares exactly one friend - the attorney. It chooses which operations and nested types become the attorney's contract, without needing to know every collaborator that will consume that contract.

The gatekeeper made friend of the client: its callable operations stay private and forward selected client members; where a collaborator needs a type, it may publish only a named nested-type alias (classically a typedef) and keep the type-access functions private to the requestor.

The helper that needs the implementation - a test harness, serializer, iterator adapter or sibling component. It calls through the attorney's narrow operations and may name only the nested types deliberately aliased for it, rather than depending on the client's whole private surface.

use_cases: White-box test access: a test harness reaches one private hook or state view through a named attorney instead of making the member public or redefining private with a test-only preprocessor switch.

Iterator adapters: Boost.Iterator's iterator_core_access is a canonical gateway class a user-defined iterator befriends, so iterator_facade and its operators reach private dereference/increment/advance core functions while those implementation hooks stay out of the iterator's public API.

Serialization: Boost.Serialization has serializable classes befriend boost::serialization::access, whose gateway reaches the private serialize() member so archives can reconstruct state without a public serialization method.

Private nested type exposure: LLVM's SchedulerInternalsAttorney publishes the selected nested Scheduler::BndlSchedState as a public type alias and supplies narrow static accessors for unit tests, without publishing every Scheduler private type.

A pImpl-backed adapter that must inspect one implementation-owned type: keep the public class opaque and put the attorney definition in the adapter or test header, so the privileged component gets a typed view without making the implementation part of the ordinary public contract.

Iterator facade over a hidden list-like representation: expose a stable nested iterator/view type through an attorney rather than publishing std::list<T>::iterator, so the owner can replace the container without promising its node and invalidation details to every caller.
Private virtual hooks: an attorney forwards one private virtual operation through a base reference, allowing the derived override to run even though friendship is not inherited.
Factory or construction control: a builder reaches one private constructor or initialization hook through an attorney, while unrelated callers still cannot construct an object through that path.

Spacecraft flight software (fsfw): LocalDpManagerAttorney keeps fetchPoolEntry and getMutexHandle as private static forwarders and befriends only LocalPoolVariable and LocalPoolVector, so the local data pool manager opens its internals to two named collaborators instead of every class that might befriend it.

Simulator tree traversal (Sandia Sparta Modeling Framework): sparta::TreeNodePrivateAttorney exposes TreeNode's private child vectors and subtrees through static accessors (getAllChildren, getChild, findChildren) for internal Reports and Pipeout processing, with a documented 'should NOT be used by simulation developers' restriction in place of an enforceable caller limit.
avoid_when: The collaborator needs the whole private interface: a single friend declaration (or package-private access) is simpler - the attorney only pays for itself when the grant is a strict subset.
The operation is a legitimate part of the type's contract: make it public or extract an interface instead of hiding it behind a gate every reader has to look up.

The language already names the exact scope: Rust's pub(in path)/pub(super), Scala's private[C], Swift's fileprivate or package access, Kotlin's file-private top level and module boundaries express the grant directly - do not hand-build an attorney class around them.
The goal is to stop untrusted callers: compile-time access control is not a security boundary; use runtime enforcement (a reference monitor, capability wrappers, complete mediation) instead.

Tests are the only reason: prefer the language's test affordance (@testable import in Swift, an internal/export_test.go alias in Go, a package-private test in Java) or plain black-box tests, and expect white-box tests to slow refactoring down.

The boundary is a translation unit in a language without access control (C) or the type is a value/data holder: the grant degenerates into file-scope linkage and the attorney adds ceremony without a checked boundary.

The codebase uses C++20 modules: the private module fragment (module :private;) creates a hard encapsulation boundary where non-exported declarations are genuinely invisible to importers - friend declarations cannot reach inside it. This makes the attorney unnecessary for module-internal privacy, though it remains useful for cross-module per-collaborator grants.

The requirement is representation hiding and ABI or recompilation isolation, not privileged collaboration: use pImpl and a stable public interface; a public attorney alias to a private nested implementation recreates the header dependency pImpl is meant to remove.

Many unrelated callers need a stable read-only view: use a wrapper or facade with an intentional public contract; an attorney is for a named collaborator and otherwise turns a private interface into an undocumented second API.

The selected nested type must itself remain unavailable to most code: a public attorney typedef cannot restrict who names the aliased type, so keep the attorney definition out of general headers or use private forwarding functions or a passkey instead.
anti_patterns: Attorney that mirrors the whole private interface: every member is forwarded and nothing is withheld, so a plain friend declaration expresses the same grant with less code; keep only a cohesive subset.

Public attorney with unrestricted forwarding: anyone who includes the header can call the gate, so the grantor's private interface has become a public API; make the forwarders private and friend only the requestor.
Over-privileged attorney: one gate accumulates unrelated clients and member groups, becoming a coupling hub; split it into cohesive attorneys or refactor the collaborators.
Two parallel grants: the requestor is still a direct friend of the grantor while an attorney exists, leaving the all-or-nothing path open; remove the direct friend after migrating calls.
Security theatre: presenting compiler access control as protection against an adversary ignores macros, reflection, debuggers and binary patching; use runtime mediation for untrusted callers.
Attorney as business logic: decisions, state or lazy initialization inside the gate turn a transparent access seam into a second component; keep it to forwarding and selected type aliases.

Attorney for C++20 module internals: using a gate for details already hidden by a private module fragment adds ceremony without selective benefit; reserve it for a collaborator grant that module visibility cannot express.
design_principles: Least privilege: hand out the smallest callable surface that lets the collaborator do its job, and nothing more.
Encapsulation and information hiding: the private implementation stays private, and only a named subset becomes reachable through a type the grantor chose.
Explicitness: the grant is a visible declaration (a friend, a dedicated attorney type, a restricted-visibility annotation) rather than a side effect of scope or of a member accidentally being public.
Single responsibility and separation of concerns: the attorney does one thing - forward the granted operations - and owns no logic of its own.
Interface segregation: the requestor depends only on the operations it actually calls, not on the grantor's type or its full private surface.
Open/closed at the boundary: the grantor's remaining private members can be refactored freely while new grants are added inside the attorney without touching the implementation.
best_practices: Make operation forwarders private and expose only intentionally selected nested-type aliases; befriend the requestor from the attorney rather than the grantor when the requestor must invoke those forwarders, so the grantor keeps exactly one friend.

Forward, do not implement: the attorney holds no state and no logic, each operation is a single delegating call, and each public typedef names an existing client type rather than introducing a second implementation.

Keep the grant small and cohesive: prefer several attorneys for disjoint subsets over one attorney that forwards everything - if the attorney reaches most of the grantor, the boundary is wrong, so split the type or extract an interface.
Prefer the attorney over blanket friendship whenever the collaborator needs less than everything, and write down next to the friend declaration why the grant exists and who is expected to use it.

Keep the forwarded signatures in one place where the language allows it (a templated attorney re-exporting members with using-declarations, a single forwarding header) so a signature change cannot drift silently.

Do not put a private implementation type in a broad public signature by accident: an intentional attorney typedef is the exception, and it must live in a header whose distribution matches the collaborator set; otherwise use an opaque public type or forwarding function.
State in the code or the documentation that the boundary is compile-time encapsulation against accident, and keep runtime mediation for untrusted callers.
Add a static_assert near the attorney declaration documenting its purpose and the client class it gates, so future maintainers understand why the pattern was chosen over a direct friend declaration.

For per-method access grants in C++11 and later, prefer the passkey idiom (an unforgeable token type with a private constructor) over the attorney: it requires no separate helper class, and each method independently controls its own callers by requiring an instance of the key.

Avoid concept-constrained friend declarations (friend void f() requires C<T>) in Clang-based compilers due to open bugs (llvm/llvm-project#58859, #145505) where private access fails during constraint checking. Use unconstrained friend templates or apply concepts at the call site only.

In C++20 codebases, prefer the private module fragment (module :private;) for module-internal privacy; reserve the attorney for cross-module per-collaborator grants that cannot be expressed with module partitions alone.
sources: Bolton, Alan R. (January 2006) 'Friendship and the Attorney-Client Idiom', C/C++ Users Journal / Dr. Dobb's Journal. Original article that coined and formalised the idiom, including variations (Corporate Counsel, Consigliere) and guidelines on when friendship is justified.

Márton, Gábor and Porkoláb, Zoltán (2018) 'Selective friends in C++', Software: Practice and Experience, 48(8), pp. 1493-1519. Empirical study of friendship usage in open-source C++ projects; finds frequent misuse and over-granting; proposes a language-level selective friend construct. DOI: 10.1002/spe.2587. URL: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/spe.2587

P2893R3 (2024) 'Variadic friends', ISO C++ Working Group (WG21). Proposes friend Ts... syntax for C++26 to befriend multiple types in one declaration; discusses Passkey idiom limitations and attorney-client as the pattern-based workaround. URL: https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2024/p2893r3.html

std-proposals (2024) 'Improving Friends with Attributes'. Proposes [[selective_access]] attribute on friend declarations to restrict access to named private members, combined with [[const_access]] for read-only variants. Proof-of-concept: martong/clang/selective_friend. URL: https://groups.google.com/a/isocpp.org/g/std-proposals/c/wtkDvujmjug

Chromium PassKey pattern documentation. Describes base::PassKey<T>, Chromium's production use of the passkey idiom (a C++11 refinement of attorney-client per-method access). URL: https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/HEAD/docs/patterns/passkey.md

llvm/llvm-project (2024) 'Unable to friend a function with concept or requires clause', Clang bug #58859. Documents a compiler bug where constrained friend templates fail private member access during constraint checking in Clang; similar issues at #61823, #63536, #145505.

C++20 Modules documentation, cppreference. Documents private module fragment (module :private;) which creates a hard encapsulation boundary where non-exported declarations are genuinely invisible to importers, superseding many attorney use cases for module-internal privacy. URL: https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/language/modules

Márton, Gábor (2019) PhD Thesis: 'Tools and Language Elements for Testing, Encapsulation and Controlling Abstraction in Large Scale C++ Projects', Eötvös Loránd University. Critically analyses attorney-client, proposes selective friend language feature; covers non-intrusive testing techniques and access key idioms. URL: https://martong.github.io/gabor-marton-phd-thesis.pdf

fsfw flight software framework, LocalDpManagerAttorney.h. Production use of the attorney-client idiom: private static forwarders fetchPoolEntry/getMutexHandle with only LocalPoolVariable and LocalPoolVector befriended, documented as more granular and encapsulated than direct friend declarations. URL: https://egit.irs.uni-stuttgart.de/mohr/fsfw/src/commit/efc2773f841e2a8e4856f3b2507142d5cb631e94/src/fsfw/datapoollocal/internal/LocalDpManagerAttorney.h

Sandia Sparta Modeling Framework, sparta::TreeNodePrivateAttorney class reference. A production attorney exposing TreeNode private subtrees to internal framework processing (Reports, Pipeout), with an explicit documentation-only 'should NOT be used by simulation developers' restriction. URL: https://sparcians.github.io/map/classsparta_1_1TreeNodePrivateAttorney.html

Boost.Iterator documentation, 'Iterator Facade and Adaptor'. Official description of the trapdoor design where iterator_core_access reaches a derived iterator's private core operations (dereference, increment, advance) so the facade's public interface stays clean. URL: https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/latest/libs/iterator/doc/facade-and-adaptor.html

Boost.Serialization documentation, 'Serialization of Classes'. The recommended grant form: keep serialize() private and declare friend class boost::serialization::access so archives can save/load state without a public serialization entry point. URL: https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/latest/libs/serialization/doc/serialization.html

Stack Overflow, 'clean C++ granular friend equivalent?'. Discussion naming the attorney-client idiom as the granular-friend mechanism and weighing it against the passkey idiom and blanket friendship tradeoffs. URL: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/3217390/clean-c-granular-friend-equivalent-answer-attorney-client-idiom

related_patterns_notes.passkey: Passkey requires a caller to possess an unforgeable token for each operation; attorney-client grants a selected operation or nested type through a friend-mediated surface.
related_patterns_notes.pimpl: pImpl hides representation behind an opaque pointer for ABI and recompilation isolation; attorney-client intentionally grants one collaborator access to a selected private contract.
related_patterns_notes.nvi: Non-Virtual Interface keeps a public nonvirtual template method above private virtual hooks; an attorney is an access gate for a collaborator, not a dispatch policy.
related_patterns_notes.policy-based-design: Policy-based design composes behavior through template parameters; attorney-client controls which existing private behavior a named collaborator may reach.
related_patterns_notes.proxy: Proxy substitutes a separate object and may add remote or lazy behavior; attorney-client is normally stateless compile-time forwarding or type exposure around the same client.
related_patterns_notes.least-privilege: Least privilege is the governing principle; attorney-client is one C++ mechanism for applying it to friend access, not a runtime authorization system.
related_patterns_notes.subclass-sandbox: Subclass sandbox grants protected access through inheritance and a restricted subclass; attorney-client avoids claiming an is-a relationship and mediates selected private members instead.
